title: Greening (Hildegard)
hookLine: Hildegard's word for the green life of God in creation
tomorrow: who calls death a sister, and means it kindly?

lines: A NEW SHOOT AT THE WINDOW.
cards: A houseplant left in a dark corner goes pale and limp. Nobody meant to neglect it; life just got busy. Move it to the window, water it, and soon there's a new shoot, bright and soft and cool to the touch.
So what color is a soul that's coming back to life? For an abbess named Hildegard, the answer was green. She had a word for what returns to that plant, and she used it for people too.

teach.b: First, the word. Viriditas is plain Latin for greenness. In Hildegard's writing it grows far past a color.

Second, creation. She uses it for the fresh, wet, growing life in the world: sap rising in the branch, the sprout pushing up in the field, the smell of cut grass, everything alive and reaching toward light.
In her reading, that life comes from God and keeps flowing from God. Third, the soul. Hildegard turns the same word inward.

teach.h: A SOUL CAN GO GREEN, OR WITHER.
teach.b: A person can be green, full of fresh life and good works, and a person can dry out and wither, she writes, when that life is neglected.
Holiness, in her picture, looks less like polished stone and more like a watered garden after rain. Fourth, Mary.
In one of her songs Hildegard greets Mary as the greenest branch, O viridissima virga, the branch that flowered with Christ.
The word she used for a leaf, she gives to the mother of God. Hildegard was a visionary, a composer and a healer, and the Church now counts her among its Doctors.
And this one green word runs all through her writing, from the field to the soul to the song.

how: Catholics honor Hildegard of Bingen as a saint and Doctor of the Church; her songs are still sung, and her writings are read for their visions of creation.

o: a Latin name for the herbs used in healing
the fresh, green life of God in creation
the green robes worn by abbesses at prayer

s: viriditas, for Hildegard, just means the color green
she uses it for the fresh, growing life of God in creation and in souls.
Hildegard writes that a soul can dry out and wither when that life is neglected
and green life can come back.
Hildegard wrote only about plants and medicine
she was a visionary and a composer, and gave her green word to souls and to Mary.

games.q: your uncle's been flat since he retired: no projects, nobody over, the curtains shut. which of Hildegard's pictures fits, and what does it suggest?
o: a plant in a dark corner: with light and care, life can come back green.
a polished stone: some people are simply finished growing.
a fallen leaf: better to let the season end on its own.
games.why: for Hildegard a soul can wither when its fresh life is neglected, and that life comes from God and keeps flowing. greening is what returns.

practice: If there's a plant near you, rest a fingertip on one leaf and feel how cool and alive it is; if you can, smell it. If not, look at the nearest green thing outside, or bring a tree you know to mind.
Breathe slowly, and let Hildegard's word sit there with you: viriditas.

wordCard.voice: Viriditas. Hildegard's greening: the fresh life of God in leaves, in fields, in a song for Mary, and in people.

orig.note: Latin for greenness: Hildegard's word for the fresh life of God in creation and in souls.

carryVoice: Carry this: greening, the hope that a dried-out soul can turn green and alive again, the way a pale plant does by the window. Back tomorrow.
